topic_summary: This menu covers the key tax considerations for Australian rental property owners, grounded in ATO guidance (snapshot 8223d8c0-de90-4c5a-a9cc-2890a245684e). Topics span capital gains tax on disposal, record-keeping obligations (including the 5-year retention rule after a CGT event), PAYG instalments (triggered at $4,000 rental income or a tax debt above $1,000, with 2 quarterly options), value shifting rules (applying where market value exceeds consideration by more than $50,000), and the cashflow timing gap between ongoing rental losses and the eventual tax saving — a gap no competitor adequately addresses.

terminals.heading: I sold (or am selling) my rental property — do I have a capital gain or loss?
terminals.result_copy: A CGT event is indicated to occur when you enter into the contract of sale (not at settlement) for a rental property acquired after 19 September 1985. Your capital gain would be calculated as the capital proceeds minus the cost base; a capital loss is indicated if the reduced cost base exceeds the proceeds. Co-owners would calculate their gain or loss according to their ownership interest. Certain rollovers may allow the gain or loss to be disregarded. Review recommended to confirm the applicable cost base components and any rollover eligibility for your specific situation.

terminals.heading: How long must I keep records for my rental property's CGT?
terminals.result_copy: Records of everything that affects your capital gains and capital losses — including all costs of acquiring, holding and disposing of the property — are required to be kept. Penalties can apply if records are not kept for at least 5 years after the relevant CGT event. Review recommended to confirm which specific records apply to your property's history.

terminals.heading: Will I need to pay PAYG instalments because of my rental income?
terminals.result_copy: PAYG instalments are generally indicated to apply if rental or other investment income is $4,000 or more, or if the debt on an income tax assessment is more than $1,000. If paying quarterly, there are usually 2 options available. Whether the threshold is met in your case depends on your actual income and tax debt figures — review recommended to confirm your obligation and the instalment options available to you.

terminals.heading: Could granting a lease to an associate before I sell trigger the value-shifting rules?
terminals.result_copy: The general value shifting regime is indicated as a potential consideration where a lease is granted to an associate before entering a contract of sale, and the lease was originally created on non-commercial terms such that the market value of the right was greater than what was received for creating it by more than $50,000. Whether the rules apply depends on the specific terms of the lease and the relationship with the associate. Professional advice is recommended to determine whether value shifting applies and what the CGT consequences would be.

terminals.heading: What counts as the cost base of my rental property for CGT purposes?
terminals.result_copy: The cost base of a rental property generally includes the amount paid for the property plus certain incidental costs to acquire, hold and dispose of it (for example, legal fees, stamp duty and real estate agent commissions). Certain amounts that have been deducted or can be deducted are excluded from the cost base, as are travel expenses relating to a residential rental property. The correct cost base components depend on the specific costs incurred and deductions claimed — review recommended to confirm what is included or excluded in your case.

terminals.heading: Can I get my negative-gearing tax benefit in each pay cycle instead of waiting until my tax return?
terminals.result_copy: Where a rental property is negatively geared (rental income is less than deductible expenses including interest on borrowings), a net rental loss may arise and a deduction for the full amount of rental expenses may be claimable against rental and other income when completing a tax return. A PAYG withholding variation may allow the tax benefit of that rental loss to be reflected in each pay cycle rather than waiting until the annual tax return. The PAYG instalment system — which applies once rental income reaches $4,000 or the tax debt exceeds $1,000 — is the formal mechanism through which this timing can be managed. Whether a variation is available and appropriate depends on individual circumstances — review recommended.

terminals.heading: How does my marginal tax rate affect the actual tax saving from my rental loss?
terminals.result_copy: Negative gearing occurs when rental income is less than deductible expenses (including interest on borrowings), producing a net rental loss. That loss may be claimable as a deduction against rental and other income (such as salary, wages or business income) when completing a tax return for the relevant income year. Where other income is not sufficient to absorb the loss, it may be carried forward to the next income year. How this interacts with a marginal tax rate depends on individual income levels and circumstances — review recommended to assess the tax effect in your specific situation.
